1.sense: The address opens to the Prophet ﷺ but the instruction that follows is plural, spoken to the whole community through him. Divorce is to be pronounced at the start of a waiting period a woman can complete in full, and that count is to be kept exactly. She is not put out of her house during it, nor does she leave on her own, unless she commits a clear indecency. These are called the limits of Allah, and stepping past them is a wrong a person does to himself.

notes.t: The verb ṭallaqtumu is plural though the opening address, yā-ayyuhā an-nabiyyu, names the Prophet ﷺ alone; the surah speaks through him to every husband bound by the rule that follows.
The waiting period this verse tells husbands to count in full is set out earlier as three menstrual courses for most women.
Exegetes differ on what the clear indecency permitting a woman's removal refers to here: some read it as open sexual immorality, others as vile speech or open defiance toward the husband's household.
notes.src: al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir record both readings

links.why: the identical exception, a clear indecency, permits withholding something owed a wife elsewhere, there her dower rather than her housing
the same phrase, the limits of Allah, closing the Qur'an's general legislation on divorce and its revocation

2.sense: The waiting period reaching its end forces a choice: keep the marriage on fair terms or let it end on fair terms, with no lingering to cause harm either way. Two just witnesses are to be brought in and the testimony given for Allah's sake, not for either party to the marriage. The instruction is tied to real belief, in Allah and the Last Day, and closes with a promise, whoever is mindful of Allah is given a way out.

notes.t: Maʿrūf, the recognized and decent way, appears twice in one clause: whichever choice is made, retaining or releasing, is to be carried out to the same standard.
The two just witnesses called for here use the same phrase set earlier for debt contracts, extending a rule built for commerce to a marriage's revocation or end.
Jurists differ on whether taking witnesses to a divorce or its revocation is a condition for validity or simply recommended; most held it recommended, not required.
notes.src: al-Shafiʿi and others held it obligatory; the majority of jurists held it recommended

links.why: the same fork, retain in kindness or release, with an added warning there against retaining a wife only to harm her

words.g: and He will provide for him

3.sense: The promise of a way out continues into provision from a source not reckoned on. Trust placed in Allah is met with sufficiency, because Allah's reach covers whatever He sets in motion. The verse closes on a general principle: everything Allah has made carries a measure already fixed for it.

notes.t: Yaḥtasibu, to reckon or calculate, and ḥasbuhu, sufficient, share the same root ḥ-s-b; the verse sets one kind of reckoning against another, what a person could count on is not the source of what actually reaches him.
The same idea, provision reaching someone from where they had not reckoned, is shown rather than stated in the story of Zakariyya finding Maryam supplied with food he had not brought her.

links.why: the same pattern shown as a narrative, provision reaching Maryam from where Zakariyya did not expect it

4.sense: The three-month count is extended to two groups the general rule could not settle on its own: women past their courses and women who have not yet begun them. For a pregnant woman the term is fixed by an event, delivery, rather than by counting months at all. The refrain about ease for the mindful, already given once in this passage, closes the ruling a second time.

notes.t: This verse fills gaps the earlier count by menstrual courses leaves open: menopause, a girl who has not yet menstruated, and pregnancy, each given its own way of marking the term.
The four months and ten days set for a widow's waiting period is a separate count from the three months legislated here for a living husband's divorce.

Jurists differ over a pregnant woman whose husband dies during her waiting period: whether her term ends at delivery regardless, or only once both delivery and the widow's four months and ten days have passed.
notes.src: the majority held delivery alone ends it; a minority required the longer of the two

links.why: the parallel term set for widows, a different count from the three months used here

5.sense: What has just been legislated is named directly: a command sent down from Allah, not custom or convention. Mindfulness of Allah is tied to a reward again, framed this time as sins wiped away and a reward made greater, alongside the way out and the ease already promised twice before it.

notes.t: Amru llāhi, the command of Allah, closes the ruling by naming its source plainly, echoing the earlier phrase the limits of Allah that opened the same instruction.
The same pairing, bad deeds removed and a reward magnified, is made elsewhere conditional on avoiding the major sins one has been forbidden.

links.why: the same promise, minor bad deeds wiped away, tied there to avoiding the major ones

6.sense: Provision for a divorced woman is set out in practical terms: housing at the standard the husband can afford, with no pressure used to force her out. Full maintenance continues through a pregnancy until she delivers, and if she nurses the child afterward she is paid a wage for it. Any disagreement over nursing is to be resolved by consultation, or failing that by finding another woman to nurse the child.

notes.t: Tuḍāyyiqū, to straiten, sits next to tuḍārrūhunna, to harm; the ban named here is financial pressure used as leverage against a woman still owed housing, not merely unkind treatment.

The fuller rule behind the wage for nursing and the call to settle disputes over it by consultation between the parents is given earlier, with the added principle that neither parent is to be harmed on the child's account.

links.why: the fuller legislation on nursing wages and parental consultation that this verse condenses

7.sense: The spending obligation scales to means: the well-off spend from their abundance, the constrained spend from what they have actually been given, and no one is charged beyond that. The refrain returns a third time, promising ease after hardship, closing the passage on divorce and maintenance with the same words that opened its middle.

notes.t: A way out, then ease, then ease after hardship: the same promise to the mindful is given three times across this passage, each time in slightly different words.
No soul is charged beyond what it has been given restates a general principle given elsewhere for religious duties as a whole, not only for spending on a divorced wife.

links.why: the same principle, no soul is burdened beyond what it is given, stated there for duties in general
the same refrain, ease coming after hardship, repeated twice in that surah

words.g: so We called it to account

8.sense: The register shifts from instruction to warning, and the address moves from a person to a town, the Qur'an's usual stand-in for a rejecting community. Defiance against Allah's command and the word of His messengers is met with a strict reckoning first, then a harsh punishment, the sequence moving from account taken to consequence delivered.

notes.t: Qaryah, town, names no particular people; the warning is left general rather than pinned to one story, so it reads as a pattern rather than a single history.
The same opening words, how many a town, introduce elsewhere a community given time before its reckoning came, rather than punished at once.

links.why: the same opening words, how many a town, used there for a community given time before the reckoning came

9.sense: The consequence lands in two words, tasting and outcome: the town tasted the weight of its own defiance, and what followed it was loss rather than any gain. The sentence is short, matching the abruptness of the ending it describes.

notes.t: Dhāqat, tasted, is the Qur'an's habitual verb for suffering a consequence directly rather than merely hearing of it; wabāl is the weight a choice leaves behind on the one who made it.
The identical phrase, tasting the weight of its own affair, is used for the peoples of Nuh, 'Ad and Thamud after each rejected its messenger.

links.why: the identical phrase, tasting the weight of its own affair, used there for the peoples of Nuh, 'Ad and Thamud

10.sense: Allah has prepared a severe punishment for the defiant town, and the address turns back to the living, calling on people of understanding who believe to be mindful of Allah. What has already been sent down, called a reminder here, is the legislation on divorce and maintenance the surah has just laid out.

notes.t: Dhikran, a reminder, names what has just been given: the surah calls its own legal instruction a reminder, the same word used elsewhere for the Qur'an as a whole.
The reminder is named again as something Allah has sent down and undertaken to guard, describing the Qur'an as a whole rather than one ruling within it.

links.why: the same word, a reminder, used there for the Qur'an as a whole rather than one ruling within it

11.sense: The reminder is given a shape: a messenger reciting clear verses, sent to bring believers out of darkness and into light. Whoever believes and acts rightly is admitted to gardens with rivers running beneath them, to remain there always, with provision Allah has made excellent for him.

notes.t: The darknesses are plural, ẓulumāt, against a single light, an-nūr; the same pairing, many wrong ways set against one right one, recurs across several surahs.
The same phrase, bringing people out of the darknesses into the light, opens another surah's description of what the Qur'an was sent down to do.

links.why: the same phrase, out of the darknesses into the light, opening that surah's description of the Qur'an's purpose

12.sense: The closing verse widens the frame from one household's law to the architecture of creation: seven heavens, and a like number reckoned of the earth, with the command descending between them. What is stated is Allah's power over everything and knowledge encompassing everything, the same two claims the surah's rulings have been resting on throughout.

notes.t: Mithlahunna, the like of them, is read as seven earths corresponding to the seven heavens; the verse names the count without describing what those earths are like.
The seven heavens named here as created in layers are described that way, one raised above another, in another surah's opening call to look upward.

A hadith has the Prophet ﷺ say that whoever wrongfully seizes a hand-span of land will be made, on the Day of Rising, to carry it down through seven earths, taking the seven earths named here as real and stacked.
notes.src: Bukhari and Muslim, from Saʿid ibn Zayd

links.why: the seven heavens in layers, the same count named here without description
